projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: A cable came today from Mr Quinn, New York. He offers to buy from me the proof sheets of my novel with my corrections thereon, at present in the hands of my American publisher, for £20 (twenty pounds) which sum he says he will transmit to me by cable on receipt of my cabled acceptance. I have therefore telegraphed to you to cable him my acceptance and send you M.O (10/-) which I hope will cover your expenses. I think this is better than cabling from here. Many thanks in advance. I am getting better, I think, but am still under doctor’s care. He speaks always of an operation

div.note: cf. related letter in Letters I 100 – to Quinn, same date

In late January 1917, JJ and family moved from Seefeldstrasse 54 to Seefeldstrasse 73, where they remained until October 1917. The new flat, on the third floor with two large rooms facing the street, was offered to JJ by his pupil, Paul Ruggiero, a bank employee whose father had formerly occupied the premises. JJ found it more comfortable but also much more expensive than their previous place. Adjoining rooms formed a separate flat occupied by Philipp Jarnach (1892-1982), student of and secretary to the composer Ferruccio Busoni (1866-1924). Jarnach himself was a composer and later became a teacher of composition. Though he was initially disturbed by JJ’s singing and untuned piano, they became friendly and discussed music and other subjects (Ellmann, JJ 408-09).

The New York lawyer John Quinn (1870-1924) was an important collector of modern art and literary manuscripts. He sent a cable to JJ on 13 March 1917 (at JJ’s former address; hence the delay, perhaps) about the “good success” that A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man was having with reviewers. He also offered to cable JJ “twenty pounds for sheets Egoist and page manuscript addition with interlineations and corrections by you, used by Huebsch for printing book” (Pound/Joyce 289). JJ accepted this offer in a letter to Quinn dated 19 March 1917 and asked Pound to cable the acceptance to Quinn as well (LI 100).
When B.W. Huebsch of New York published the American edition of A Portrait in December 1916, he had the text set from the pages of the novel that had appeared serially in the London magazine The Egoist (1914-1915), with corrections and additions in JJ’s hand. (These pages are now at Yale.) These were the pages for which Quinn offered £20. A comic lawyerly brawl preceded JJ’s receipt of the money. Huebsch had given the pages to E. Byrne Hackett (1879-1953), a bookstore owner and director of the Yale University Press, who had been at Clongowes school with young JJ. Quinn thought that neither Huebsch nor Byrne had any right to JJ’s pages and resented Byrne’s attempt to take a commission on their sale to Quinn. After a flurry of threats and recriminations, Hackett haughtily surrendered, gave the pages to Huebsch, who gave them to Quinn. Quinn sent the £20 to Pound, who sent it to JJ. Boasting of his victory over Hackett, whom he considered a bad sort of Irishman, Quinn sent Pound the file of his correspondence with Hackett and Huebsch over the matter (Pound/Joyce 287-300). Quinn summed up the affair to the New York publisher Mitchell Kennerley (1878-1950) in a letter dated 15 November 1918: “If there ever was a man nailed for cupidity Mr. Hackett was there” (John Quinn Memorial Collection, New York Public Library, Manuscripts & Archives Division).

See JJ to Pound, 19 March 1917, for the text of the cable that JJ sent to Pound. On 28 March 1917, Pound wrote JJ: “Rec’d your money order for 10/. I forget how much the cable was, but I think I owe you 3/ change, which I will send along with the £20 when it arrives” (Pound/Joyce 103).

Shortly after moving to Seefeldstrasse 73, JJ had a painful attack of glaucoma and synechia, diseases of the retina that can lead to blindness. The attack lasted into March 1917 and recurred in April. At this time, JJ was resisting his doctor’s suggestion of an operation, which would involve removal of portions of the iris (Ellmann, JJ 412).
